About: Wire and Solenoid — One Field Thins Out, the Other Does Not

Source

Topic
Magnetic field of a long straight wire and a long solenoid (Ampère's law)
Concept
The straight wire's field falls as 1/r; a long solenoid's interior field is uniform, set only by n and I.
Audience
JEE / NCERT Class 11–12 — Moving Charges & Magnetism
Inquiry
Three gated predictions, then a comparison: doubling the distance from the wire halves B; moving the probe inside the solenoid changes B not at all; and doubling n while halving I leaves the interior field where it was.
Misconception
"Magnetic fields fall off as 1/r², like Coulomb's law." — false for a straight wire (1/r) and irrelevant inside a long solenoid (independent of position).

1 · Two ways to make a magnetic field

Left: a long straight wire seen end-on, its current I coming out of the page; the blue circles are its magnetic field lines. Right: the same current wound into a long solenoid, cut open lengthwise, with the field inside drawn as pink arrows. A yellow probe in each panel reports the magnetic field B at its own position.

3 · Moving inside the solenoid

In the solenoid you double the turns per metre n and at the same time halve the current I. The field inside becomes:

Long straight wire

Ampère's law on a circle of radius r around the wire. Falls as 1/r — not 1/r².

Long solenoid, inside

Ampère's law on a rectangular loop straddling the winding. Depends only on n (turns/m) and I — not on where you stand or the solenoid's radius.

Force on 1 m of wire carrying I, inside the solenoid

If the wire crosses the axis (θ = π/2), the force per metre is BI. This is the force reported by the audit hook.

μ₀

Permeability of free space. The engine carries the CODATA value 1.25663706212×10⁻⁶ T·m/A, which agrees with 4π×10⁻⁷ to nine figures.

01

At a glance

Two pictures share one current. On the left is a long straight wire seen end-on, and on the right is a long solenoid cut open lengthwise. A yellow probe in each panel reads the magnetic field B where it sits.

What you'll learn

  • How the field of a straight wire depends on the distance from the wire and on the current.
  • How the field inside a solenoid depends on where you measure it, on the turns per metre n and on the current.
  • How Ampère's law gives both fields.

03

A long straight wire's field falls as 1/r

The field lines are circles around the wire, and B has the same size all round a circle of radius r. In the sim the current comes out of the page, and the field circles counterclockwise: thumb along the current, fingers curl along B. Its size is

B = μ₀ I / (2π r)
μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A. B is in tesla for I in amperes and r in metres.

B is inversely proportional to r. It is not 1/r². Doubling r halves B. At I = 10 A, μ₀I/2π = 2 × 10⁻⁶ T·m, so:

r (cm)24581020
B (µT)1005040252010
See itPut the wire probe at r = 4 cm, then move it to r = 8 cm. Watch for: the wire reading B = 50.00 µT at 4 cm, then 25.00 µT at 8 cm.
04

Inside a long solenoid, B is the same everywhere

Inside a long solenoid the field points along the axis and has the value

B = μ₀ n I
n is the number of turns per metre.
  • Only n and I appear. The distance from the axis and the solenoid's radius do not.
  • At n = 1000 /m and I = 10 A, B = 12.566 mT, over 300 times the wire's 40.00 µT at 5 cm.
  • Right-hand rule: curl the fingers along the winding current and the thumb gives B. Here that is to the right.
  • Outside the windings the field of a long solenoid is close to zero. The sim shows this as "≈ 0 (outside)".
See itSlide the solenoid probe from the axis up to 15 cm from it. Watch for: the solenoid reading staying at 12.566 mT while the probe moves.
05

The solenoid's field depends on the product n I

Since B = μ₀ n I, doubling n doubles B and doubling I doubles B. Doubling n while halving I leaves n I, and so B, unchanged.

  • n = 1000 /m with I = 10 A, n = 2000 /m with I = 5 A and n = 500 /m with I = 20 A all give B = 12.566 mT.
  • The sliders reach from 0.251 mT (n = 200 /m, I = 1 A) to 113.097 mT (n = 3000 /m, I = 30 A).
  • The current slider is shared. Halving I halves the wire's field too, so at r = 5 cm it falls from 40.00 µT to 20.00 µT.

So the two probes respond differently to the same change in I. The solenoid's reading depends on n as well, and the wire's reading does not depend on n at all.

See itDouble n to 2000 /m, then halve I to 5.0 A. Watch for: the solenoid reading unchanged at 12.566 mT, while the wire reading falls from 40.00 to 20.00 µT.
06

Ampère's law gives both results

Ampère's law says that B added up along a closed loop, B along the path times the path length, equals μ₀ times the current through the loop.

Left: a circle of radius r around the wire. Right: a rectangle across the winding, with one side of length ℓ inside the coil.
  • Wire. B × 2πr = μ₀ I. The loop gets longer with r while the enclosed current stays I, so B = μ₀I/(2πr).
  • Solenoid. The inside side gives Bℓ. The outside side gives about 0, and the two ends are at right angles to B. The loop encloses n ℓ turns, so Bℓ = μ₀ n ℓ I, which gives B = μ₀ n I. The inside side can sit at any distance from the axis.
See itTake the solenoid probe from the axis out through the windings. Watch for: 12.566 mT inside, then "≈ 0 (outside)" once the probe leaves the coil.
07

Where it matters

  • Ørsted's compass. In 1820 a compass needle near a current-carrying wire turned, the first sign that currents make magnetic fields. The circles in the left panel are that pattern.
  • Cables. A 10 A cable gives 40 µT at 5 cm, the same order as the Earth's field of about 25 to 65 µT, so a compass placed that close to a heavy cable can be thrown off.
  • Electromagnets and MRI. A solenoid makes a strong, steady field in its middle, set by n and I. MRI scanners use a large solenoid for a uniform field inside the bore.
Go deeper: how long is "long"

B = μ₀ n I is the limit of a very long coil. The coil drawn here is a little over 3 times longer than it is wide. For a coil of that shape, the on-axis field is about 0.96 of μ₀nI at the centre and about 0.50 of it at an end. The sim uses the ideal value everywhere inside.

08

Summary

In one line. Ampère's law gives the magnetic field of a long straight wire and of a long solenoid, and the sim lets you probe both with the same current.

Key points

  • Long straight wire: B = μ₀I/(2πr), so B ∝ 1/r, with circular field lines.
  • Long solenoid, inside: B = μ₀nI, the same at every point, and close to zero outside.
  • The wire's field depends on I and r. The solenoid's depends on n I.
  • Both come from Ampère's law with a well-chosen loop.

Common mix-ups

  • "Magnetic fields fall off as 1/r², like Coulomb's law." A long straight wire's field falls as 1/r.
  • "Inside a solenoid the field is weaker away from the axis." In a long solenoid it is the same everywhere inside.
  • "Doubling the turns doubles the field." Only if the current stays the same. B depends on n I.

Things to try on your own

  • At I = 10 A, find the distance r at which the wire reads 25 µT.
  • At I = 1 A, find the n at which the solenoid reads closest to 1 mT.
  • Set I = 30 A and r = 2 cm, then find an n that gives the solenoid a reading near the wire's.
